title: Real Estate Vs Stocks - Which One Will Make You Richer? (Shocking Math)

dimension_notes.1_audience_topic_demand: EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE: no demand series stored. Rent/buy/invest is a broad evergreen decision topic.
dimension_notes.2_differentiated_angle: Behavioural reframing (forced savings and illiquidity as the hidden variable) over the standard returns comparison.
dimension_notes.3_title: Question plus "(Shocking Math)" parenthetical; clear, standard.
dimension_notes.4_thumbnail: Stored 480x360 copy (letterboxed): cartoon man with alarmed expression, bold "YOU'RE CHOOSING WRONG", house with green glow versus crossed-out red stock chart. Legible at mobile size, but the picture endorses the house while the opening data favours stocks. Character resembles a well-known cartoon father; rights not judged.
dimension_notes.5_opening: Paradox-first; strong; compresses 30-year and century figures.
dimension_notes.6_loops: Many mini-loops; factor reveal delayed to the end; payoff narrower than setup.
dimension_notes.7_spine: Long but well-sequenced argument; two scenario sections then a framework.
dimension_notes.9_emotion_credibility: Energetic and humorous; credibility reduced by internal arithmetic errors and an impossible timeline, helped by several checkable sources.
dimension_notes.10_ending_cta: Like and subscribe plus a not-a-financial-advisor disclaimer.
dimension_notes.11_metadata_seo: Only title and first words judged; description not assessed.

financial_checks.result: $1,945,684 at 10.4%; $1,744,940 at 10.0%. The stated rate and the result disagree.

financial_checks.claim: Housing 4% for 30 years is "about 324,000"; ratio "5.4 times"
Stocks beat housing "five times over the last 100 years"
financial_checks.result: At 10.4% versus 4% over 100 years the ratio is about 392x; five times is the 30-year figure.
CONTRADICTED: 19.5% and 29.5% on the stated numbers.

financial_checks.claim: $80,000 down on $400,000 and a 20% price drop leaves zero equity
Property tax 1.1% of $400,000 is $4,400; 1% maintenance is $4,000
Median renter vs owner net worth $10,400 vs $396,000 = 38x
financial_checks.result: 38.1x arithmetic holds; the Fed SCF 2022 source is recalled, not re-verified.

financial_checks.claim: Rental $400,000, $2,500 rent, 20% down at 7%: about -$11,500 a year, -14.5% cash on cash
financial_checks.result: P&I $2,129/month ($25,545/year); with 1.1% tax, $2,500 insurance, 1% maintenance and an assumed 8% vacancy and 8% management, cash flow is about -$11,200; -14% on $80,000. Consistent but excludes appreciation and principal.

financial_checks.claim: Friend one: $80,000 grows to about $1.4 million in 30 years; friend two house $400,000 to $1.1 million
financial_checks.result: $1.396M at 10.0% nominal; house CAGR 3.4%. Neither adjusts for inflation, and the rent versus ownership cash-flow difference that drives the comparison is never given.

financial_checks.claim: "Average self-made millionaire" buys at 1.49x income; recommended for $70-100K earners
financial_checks.result: 1.49x of $70-100K is $104,300-$149,000, well below the video's own median home price of $408,000; the advice is not reconciled with its own market numbers.

financial_checks.claim: Fidelity: 537,000 401(k) millionaires, average age 59, 26 years in plan
financial_checks.result: Matches Fidelity Q4 2024 (537,000, up 27%; down from 544,000 in Q3 2024). It is not the latest count for an April 2026 upload; the ">17% of income" savings rate is a Q3 2024 figure.

financial_checks.claim: Shiller: homeowners think 7% real, actual 0.4% real since 1890 (17x); DALBAR 3-5 point investor gap; Ramsey millionaire study; Case-Shiller metro falls; S&P recovery "by March 2013 including dividends" (price index regained its high in March 2013; the total-return high came earlier, recall)
financial_checks.result: Not re-verified. DALBAR's method is contested; the Shiller expectation figure may mix nominal survey expectations with a real return.

financial_checks.claim: Friend two's $400,000 house is worth "about 1.1 million" after 30 years while the video's own housing series is 4% nominal
financial_checks.result: 1.1M is a 3.4% CAGR; at the video's 4% it would be about $1.30M. Unreconciled.

strengths: Strong paradox opening with memorable, plain analogies.
Genuinely balanced conclusion with explicit conditions for each choice.
Several verifiable official figures (SCF medians, VOO expense ratio, capital-gains exclusion).
Names behaviour (panic selling, forced savings) as the deciding variable.
weaknesses: Leverage-return arithmetic does not follow its own inputs.
Thumbnail picture favours the house against the opening data.
Inconsistent yardsticks between the owner-leverage and rental sections.
Causal claim from the 38x net-worth gap ignores selection into homeownership.
contradictions: "Five times over 100 years" versus a 30-year table.
"32 today" versus investing "at 32" with panic selling in 2008 and a house bought at the 2022 peak (both already past), and a sale "in 2027" (future).
1.49x income advice versus the $408,000 median home.
$1.1M house value (3.4%) versus the video's own 4% nominal housing return ($1.30M).
improvement_opportunities: Show the leverage example as a full table (appreciation, principal, interest, tax, insurance, maintenance) so the owner return is comparable with the rental section.
Make the thumbnail match the argument, for example both icons with a question mark, or the stock chart green and the house green with "Which one?" so neither is crossed out.
State the horizon next to every comparison (30 years versus 100) and fix 1.74M to 1.95M or state 10%.
Replace the third-friend dates with relative years and add the rent-versus-ownership cash-flow inputs to the two-friend scenario.
unavailable: Source documents for Shiller, DALBAR, Ramsey and Case-Shiller metro figures
